Salesforce (CRM) closed at $226.18 in the latest trading session, marking a -1.3% move from the prior day. The stock trailed the S&P 500, which registered a daily loss of 0.51%. On the other hand, the Dow registered a gain of 0.41%, and the technology-centric Nasdaq decreased by 1.07%.

Heading into today, shares of the customer-management software developer had lost 2.35% over the past month, outpacing the Computer and Technology sector's loss of 9.88% and lagging the S&P 500's loss of 0.87%.

Market participants will be closely following the financial results of Salesforce in its upcoming release. The company's earnings per share (EPS) are projected to be $3.43, reflecting a 5.54% increase from the same quarter last year. Alongside, our most recent consensus estimate is anticipating revenue of $11.46 billion, indicating a 11.73% upward movement from the same quarter last year.

For the full year, the Zacks Consensus Estimates are projecting earnings of $16.72 per share and revenue of $46.25 billion, which would represent changes of +33.55% and +11.38%, respectively, from the prior year.

Investors should also pay attention to any latest changes in analyst estimates for Salesforce. These latest adjustments often mirror the shifting dynamics of short-term business patterns. As a result, upbeat changes in estimates indicate analysts' favorable outlook on the business health and profitability.

Our research suggests that these changes in estimates have a direct relationship with upcoming stock price performance. To take advantage of this, we've established the Zacks Rank, an exclusive model that considers these estimated changes and delivers an operational rating system.

The Zacks Rank system, which varies between #1 (Strong Buy) and #5 (Strong Sell), carries an impressive track record of exceeding expectations, confirmed by external audits, with stocks at #1 delivering an average annual return of +25% since 1988. Over the last 30 days, the Zacks Consensus EPS estimate has moved 0.03% higher. As of now, Salesforce holds a Zacks Rank of #2 (Buy).

Investors should also note Salesforce's current valuation metrics, including its Forward P/E ratio of 13.71. For comparison, its industry has an average Forward P/E of 20.3, which means Salesforce is trading at a discount to the group.

Investors should also note that CRM has a PEG ratio of 0.8 right now. This metric is used similarly to the famous P/E ratio, but the PEG ratio also takes into account the stock's expected earnings growth rate. The Internet - Software was holding an average PEG ratio of 1.27 at yesterday's closing price.

title: Will Salesforce (CRM) Beat Estimates Again in Its Next Earnings Report?

Will Salesforce (CRM) Beat Estimates Again in Its Next Earnings Report?
Zacks Equity Research
Mon, November 2, 2026 at 9:10 AM MST 3 min read
CRM
Trade CRM on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

If you are looking for a stock that has a solid history of beating earnings estimates and is in a good position to maintain the trend in its next quarterly report, you should consider Salesforce (CRM). This company, which is in the Zacks Internet - Software industry, shows potential for another earnings beat.

This customer-management software developer has seen a nice streak of beating earnings estimates, especially when looking at the previous two reports. The average surprise for the last two quarters was 52.39%.

For the last reported quarter, Salesforce came out with earnings of $5.9 per share versus the Zacks Consensus Estimate of $3.27 per share, representing a surprise of 80.43%. For the previous quarter, the company was expected to post earnings of $3.12 per share and it actually produced earnings of $3.88 per share, delivering a surprise of 24.36%.

Price and EPS Surprise

For Salesforce, estimates have been trending higher, thanks in part to this earnings surprise history. And when you look at the stock's positive Zacks Earnings ESP (Expected Surprise Prediction), it's a great indicator of a future earnings beat, especially when combined with its solid Zacks Rank.

Our research shows that stocks with the combination of a positive Earnings ESP and a Zacks Rank #3 (Hold) or better produce a positive surprise nearly 70% of the time. In other words, if you have 10 stocks with this combination, the number of stocks that beat the consensus estimate could be as high as seven.

The Zacks Earnings ESP compares the Most Accurate Estimate to the Zacks Consensus Estimate for the quarter; the Most Accurate Estimate is a version of the Zacks Consensus whose definition is related to change. The idea here is that analysts revising their estimates right before an earnings release have the latest information, which could potentially be more accurate than what they and others contributing to the consensus had predicted earlier.

Salesforce has an Earnings ESP of +0.48% at the moment, suggesting that analysts have grown bullish on its near-term earnings potential. When you combine this positive Earnings ESP with the stock's Zacks Rank #2 (Buy), it shows that another beat is possibly around the corner.

Investors should note, however, that a negative Earnings ESP reading is not indicative of an earnings miss, but a negative value does reduce the predictive power of this metric.

Many companies end up beating the consensus EPS estimate, but that may not be the sole basis for their stocks moving higher. On the other hand, some stocks may hold their ground even if they end up missing the consensus estimate.

6 Big Funds Sold Shopify Last Quarter. Should You Follow Them Before Earnings? ©@William_Potter from Getty Images via Canva, @AndreyPopov from Getty Images via Canva
Key Takeaways

Six big funds cut or sold their Shopify (SHOP:NASDAQ) stakes in the three months to June 30, and the stock is up 39% since then.

Analysts expect Shopify's earnings to more than double from 2025 to 2028, and at about 75x forward earnings the stock trades near its usual multiple since late 2023.

The same funds' Uber (UBER:NYSE) sales have worked out better, and Uber, Salesforce (CRM:NYSE) and SAP (SAP) all trade at far lower multiples with more upside to analysts' targets.

Selling Shopify before next week's Q3 report looks like a mistake, unless revenue growth or spending misses management's guidance.

When six big funds cut the same stock in the same quarter, it's fair to wonder what they saw. That's what happened to Shopify (SHOP:NASDAQ) in the three months to June 30, according to each fund's 13F for that quarter, the latest each one has filed.

The sellers haven't been rewarded yet. Shopify is up 39% since June 30, and it reports Q3 results next week.

Two of them still own plenty

Polen Capital, a $12 billion fund, cut its stake 27% to 4.58 million shares, worth $523 million at June 30. Edgewood Management, a $10 billion fund, cut its stake 32% to 4.11 million shares, worth $469 million. Even so, Shopify was still Edgewood's No. 8 holding, at 4.8% of its US stocks, and Polen's No. 11, at 4.5%.

The other four went further. ICONIQ Capital cut its stake by 89%, and Kinetic Partners Management cut 61%, which left Shopify under 1% of each fund.

Steadfast Capital Management and SurgoCap Partners sold all their shares. As of March 31, Shopify had made up about 2% of each of those two funds.

A 13F shows only what a fund held on the last day of the quarter. So we can't tell when in the quarter they sold, at what price, or why.

Their Uber sales look better

Shopify wasn't the only stock these funds cut. Polen also cut its Uber (UBER:NYSE) stake 80% to 570,063 shares, and Steadfast sold all of its Uber shares. Uber is down 12% since June 30, so those sales look like the correct call so far.

title: What Could Surprise Microsoft Stock Investors On The Upside?

What Could Surprise Microsoft Stock Investors On The Upside?
Trefis Team

GOOG
AMZN
AAPL

Trading disclosure
Image from Pixabay

For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com.

Microsoft (MSFT) stock lost 2.8%, counting dividends, in the year to October 30, 2026, while the S&P 500 returned 11.3%. The business did not stall, with fiscal Q1 2027 revenue rising 18.8% from a year earlier. Microsoft's next upside may come from contracts customers have already signed, and from demand its data centers cannot yet meet. So how much work is Microsoft still waiting to deliver?

Microsoft Has $677 Billion Of Signed Work Still Ahead

Microsoft's commercial backlog, the contracted revenue it has not yet recognized, grew 73% from a year earlier to $677 billion in fiscal Q1 2027, management said on the October 28 call. One large Azure commitment signed in the quarter accounted for part of that total. Commercial bookings fell 12% from a year earlier, a decline management tied to large Azure commitments made in the prior year. Customer demand continues to exceed available supply, management said, which suggests Microsoft could sell more cloud capacity than it has built so far.

Microsoft's cloud computing service, Azure, provides the first proof that this demand turns into sales. Azure revenue grew 48% in the quarter despite delayed capacity, and management said the growth came from Foundry and from better use of its CPUs. Foundry, the platform on which customers build AI solutions with a choice of models, now has over 120,000 customers, and its revenue more than tripled from a year earlier.

How Big Is Microsoft's Cloud Business Now?

Microsoft's Intelligent Cloud segment made up 41.5% of company revenue in fiscal 2026, the year to June 30, 2026, against 37.7% a year earlier. Management also reports Microsoft Cloud revenue, which reached $63.9 billion in fiscal Q1 2027, up 30%.

The backlog is also large relative to the whole company. Management said roughly 30% of it will be recognized as revenue in the next 12 months. That works out to about $203 billion, against $346 billion of revenue in Microsoft's last twelve months.

The stock price appears to assume part of this already. Microsoft stock returned 26.4% from May 1 to October 30, 2026, against 5.4% for the S&P 500. On October 30, the stock closed 4.0% below its highest close of the past year.

What Could Slow Microsoft's Cloud Down?

Microsoft is already waiting on capacity. Some third-party capacity it expected in fiscal Q1 2027 was delayed, and management now expects those deliveries in the second half of the fiscal year.

Building that capacity is also expensive. Microsoft spent $45.2 billion on capital projects in fiscal Q1 2027, with $39.4 billion of that paid in cash. Management expects spending of about $170 billion for calendar 2026. A day after the call, Microsoft priced $25 billion of new debt as it pursues that AI buildout. Free cash flow fell to $18.6 billion in the quarter, down from $25.7 billion a year earlier, a drop management tied to the higher capital spending. Cash from operations still rose 29% to $58 billion, management said.

5 must-read analyst questions from Everforth's Q3 earnings call

Everforth's third quarter results were well received by the market, reflecting steady revenue growth and stronger-than-expected non-GAAP profitability. Management cited sustained investment in AI, IT modernization, and cloud transformation services as key demand drivers, with CEO Theodore Hanson highlighting that "our partnerships with Workday, Salesforce, ServiceNow and other technology leaders provide us with platform expertise required to move these AI-enabled technologies into production." The quarter also benefited from robust federal contract wins, particularly in cybersecurity and national security, as well as momentum in engineering and data services for hyperscalers.

Is now the time to buy EFOR? Find out in our full research report (it's free).

Everforth (EFOR) Q3 2026 highlights:

Revenue $1.03 billion vs S&P analysts' estimates of $1.01 billion (2% year-on-year growth, 2% beat)

Adjusted EPS $1.11 vs S&P analysts' estimates of $1.04 (6.6% beat)

Adjusted EBITDA $106.3 million vs analyst estimates of $101.1 million (10.3% margin, 5.1% beat)

Revenue guidance $980 million at the midpoint for Q4 2026, below analyst estimates of $987.2 million

Adjusted EPS guidance $1.03 at the midpoint for Q4 2026, above analyst estimates of $1.02

EBITDA guidance $98 million at the midpoint for Q4 2026, in line with analyst expectations

Operating margin 5.5%, down from 6.7% in the same quarter last year

Market capitalization $1.51 billion

While we enjoy listening to the management's commentary, our favorite part of earnings calls is the analyst questions. Those are unscripted and can often highlight topics that management teams would rather avoid or topics where the answer is complicated. Here is what has caught our attention.

Our top 5 analyst questions from Everforth's Q3 earnings call

Jeffrey Silber (BMO Capital Markets) asked about hiring trends and internal cost management. President Sadasivam Iyer explained they are adding selectively in areas with strong demand and optimizing resource allocation elsewhere.

Surinder Thind (Jefferies) questioned the impact of forward-deployed engineering and global delivery. CEO Theodore Hanson and Iyer described investments in offshore capabilities, especially via Quinnox, to support a hybrid onshore/offshore delivery model.

Margaret Nolan (William Blair) inquired about growth in security services and commercial bookings. Iyer indicated that commercial security is an emerging growth vector, with federal cybersecurity expertise creating cross-segment opportunities.

Kevin McVeigh (UBS) sought clarification on client budget trends and strategic cost savings. CFO Perry detailed the seasonal impact on billable days, and Hanson outlined expectations for steady demand and normalization of cost-saving investments.

Jason Haas (Wells Fargo) asked about technology partnership expansion and the balance between AI and quantum-driven security demand. Iyer noted new partnerships (including WisdomAI), emphasizing AI as a key catalyst for security service demand, with quantum still early stage.
